## Calculus of Simple Functions

This note collects the derivatives, integrals, identities, limits and series of
the elementary functions (polynomials, exponentials and logarithms,
trigonometric and hyperbolic functions and their inverses) for quick reference.
For the general theory see [[chain-rule]], [[quotient-rule]],
[[implicit-differentiation]], [[riemann-integral]] and [[taylor-series]].
Throughout, $a>0$, $a\neq1$ is a constant, $C$ is a constant of integration and
results hold on the natural domain of the functions involved.

## Differentiation Rules

:::{.theorem data-title="Rules of Differentiation"}

For differentiable $f,g$ and constants $c_1,c_2$:

- **Linearity:** $(c_1f+c_2g)'=c_1f'+c_2g'$.
- **Product rule:** $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$.
- **Quotient rule:** $\left(\dfrac fg\right)'=\dfrac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}$ for $g\neq0$.
- **Chain rule:** $(f\circ g)'(x)=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$.
- **Inverse functions:** $(f^{-1})'(y)=\dfrac{1}{f'(x)}$ where $y=f(x)$ and
  $f'(x)\neq0$.
- **Logarithmic differentiation:** $f'=f\,(\ln f)'$ for $f>0$, useful for
  $f(x)^{g(x)}$.

:::

## Polynomials and Powers

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $\int f(x)\,dx$ |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ | $0$ | $cx+C$ |
| $x^n$, $n\neq-1$ | $nx^{n-1}$ | $\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ |
| $\dfrac1x$ | $-\dfrac1{x^2}$ | $\ln\lvert x\rvert+C$ |
| $\sqrt x$ | $\dfrac1{2\sqrt x}$ | $\dfrac23x^{3/2}+C$ |

The power rule holds for every real exponent $n$ (for $x>0$ when $n$ is not an
integer). A polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^na_kx^k$ is differentiated and integrated
termwise:
$$
\frac{d}{dx}\sum_{k=0}^na_kx^k=\sum_{k=1}^nka_kx^{k-1},\qquad
\int\sum_{k=0}^na_kx^k\,dx=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_k}{k+1}x^{k+1}+C.
$$

The binomial theorem is the main algebraic identity:
$$
(x+y)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nkx^{n-k}y^k.
$$

## Exponentials and Logarithms

### Rules

$$
a^{x+y}=a^xa^y,\quad (a^x)^y=a^{xy},\quad a^x=e^{x\ln a},
$$
$$
\ln(xy)=\ln x+\ln y,\quad\ln\frac xy=\ln x-\ln y,\quad\ln x^r=r\ln x,\quad
\log_ax=\frac{\ln x}{\ln a}.
$$

## Derivatives and Integrals

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $\int f(x)\,dx$ |
|---|---|---|
| $e^x$ | $e^x$ | $e^x+C$ |
| $e^{kx}$ | $ke^{kx}$ | $\dfrac1ke^{kx}+C$ |
| $a^x$ | $a^x\ln a$ | $\dfrac{a^x}{\ln a}+C$ |
| $\ln\lvert x\rvert$ | $\dfrac1x$ | $x\ln\lvert x\rvert-x+C$ |
| $\log_a\lvert x\rvert$ | $\dfrac1{x\ln a}$ | $\dfrac{x\ln\lvert x\rvert-x}{\ln a}+C$ |
| $x^x$ ($x>0$) | $x^x(\ln x+1)$ | |

:::{.proof data-title="Derivative of $e^x$ and $\ln x$"}

Define $e$ by $\lim_{h\to0}(e^h-1)/h=1$. Then
$$
\frac{d}{dx}e^x=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^{x+h}-e^x}{h}=e^x\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^h-1}{h}=e^x.
$$
Since $\ln$ is the inverse of $\exp$, the inverse function rule with
$y=\ln x$, $x=e^y$ gives
$$
(\ln x)'=\frac{1}{e^y}=\frac1x.
$$

:::

:::{.example data-title="Logarithmic Differentiation"}

To differentiate $f(x)=x^x$ write $\ln f=x\ln x$, so $f'/f=\ln x+1$ and
$f'=x^x(\ln x+1)$.

:::

### Growth and Limits

$$
\ln x\ll x^p\ll e^x\quad(x\to\infty,\ p>0),\qquad
\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^p}{e^x}=0,\qquad\lim_{x\to0^+}x^p\ln x=0,
$$
$$
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x}=1,\qquad\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+x)}{x}=1,\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac xn\right)^n=e^x.
$$

## Trigonometric Functions

### Identities

$$
\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1,\qquad1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x,\qquad1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x,
$$
$$
\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x},\quad\sec x=\frac1{\cos x},\quad\csc x=\frac1{\sin x},\quad\cot x=\frac1{\tan x}.
$$

**Parity and shifts:** $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, $\cos(-x)=\cos x$,
$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x$, $\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x$, and all are $2\pi$-periodic
($\tan$ is $\pi$-periodic).

**Angle addition:**
$$
\sin(x\pm y)=\sin x\cos y\pm\cos x\sin y,\qquad
\cos(x\pm y)=\cos x\cos y\mp\sin x\sin y.
$$

**Double angle and power reduction:**
$$
\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x,\qquad\cos2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=1-2\sin^2x=2\cos^2x-1,
$$
$$
\sin^2x=\frac{1-\cos2x}{2},\qquad\cos^2x=\frac{1+\cos2x}{2}.
$$

**Product to sum:**
$$
\sin x\cos y=\tfrac12[\sin(x+y)+\sin(x-y)],\quad
\cos x\cos y=\tfrac12[\cos(x-y)+\cos(x+y)],
$$
$$
\sin x\sin y=\tfrac12[\cos(x-y)-\cos(x+y)].
$$

**Euler's formula:** $e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x$, so
$\cos x=\frac{e^{ix}+e^{-ix}}{2}$ and $\sin x=\frac{e^{ix}-e^{-ix}}{2i}$.

### Special Values

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/6$ | $\pi/4$ | $\pi/3$ | $\pi/2$ | $\pi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin x$ | $0$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $\cos x$ | $1$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt2}2$ | $\tfrac12$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
| $\tan x$ | $0$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | undefined | $0$ |

### Derivatives and Integrals

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $\int f(x)\,dx$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ | $-\cos x+C$ |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ | $\sin x+C$ |
| $\tan x$ | $\sec^2x$ | $-\ln\lvert\cos x\rvert+C$ |
| $\cot x$ | $-\csc^2x$ | $\ln\lvert\sin x\rvert+C$ |
| $\sec x$ | $\sec x\tan x$ | $\ln\lvert\sec x+\tan x\rvert+C$ |
| $\csc x$ | $-\csc x\cot x$ | $-\ln\lvert\csc x+\cot x\rvert+C$ |
| $\sec^2x$ | | $\tan x+C$ |
| $\csc^2x$ | | $-\cot x+C$ |
| $\sin^2x$ | $\sin2x$ | $\dfrac x2-\dfrac{\sin2x}4+C$ |
| $\cos^2x$ | $-\sin2x$ | $\dfrac x2+\dfrac{\sin2x}4+C$ |

:::{.proof data-title="Derivative of $\sin x$ and $\tan x$"}

Using the angle addition formula,
$$
\frac{\sin(x+h)-\sin x}{h}=\sin x\,\frac{\cos h-1}{h}+\cos x\,\frac{\sin h}{h}\to\cos x
$$
as $h\to0$, since $\sin h/h\to1$ and $(\cos h-1)/h\to0$. Similarly
$(\cos x)'=-\sin x$. By the quotient rule
$$
(\tan x)'=\frac{\cos x\cos x-\sin x(-\sin x)}{\cos^2x}=\frac1{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x.
$$

:::

### Limits

$$
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1,\qquad\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\frac12,\qquad
\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x}{x}=1.
$$

## Inverse Trigonometric Functions

| $f(x)$ | Domain | $f'(x)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\arcsin x$ | $[-1,1]$ | $\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ |
| $\arccos x$ | $[-1,1]$ | $-\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ |
| $\arctan x$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ |
| $\operatorname{arccot}x$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | $-\dfrac1{1+x^2}$ |
| $\operatorname{arcsec}x$ | $\lvert x\rvert\ge1$ | $\dfrac1{\lvert x\rvert\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ |
| $\operatorname{arccsc}x$ | $\lvert x\rvert\ge1$ | $-\dfrac1{\lvert x\rvert\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ |

with $\arcsin x+\arccos x=\pi/2$. The corresponding **standard integrals** ($a>0$)
are
$$
\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\arcsin\frac xa+C,\qquad
\int\frac{dx}{a^2+x^2}=\frac1a\arctan\frac xa+C.
$$

:::{.proof data-title="Derivative of $\arctan x$"}

Let $y=\arctan x$, so $x=\tan y$. Then by the inverse function rule
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac1{\sec^2y}=\frac1{1+\tan^2y}=\frac1{1+x^2}.
$$

:::

## Hyperbolic Functions

### Definitions and Identities

$$
\sinh x=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}2,\quad\cosh x=\frac{e^x+e^{-x}}2,\quad
\tanh x=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\quad\operatorname{sech}x=\frac1{\cosh x},
$$
$$
\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad1-\tanh^2x=\operatorname{sech}^2x,
$$
$$
\sinh(x\pm y)=\sinh x\cosh y\pm\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad
\cosh(x\pm y)=\cosh x\cosh y\pm\sinh x\sinh y,
$$
$$
\sinh2x=2\sinh x\cosh x,\qquad\cosh2x=\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x.
$$

The parametrisation $(\cosh t,\sinh t)$ traces the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=1$, as
$(\cos t,\sin t)$ traces the circle. The relation to the trigonometric functions
is $\cosh x=\cos(ix)$ and $\sinh x=-i\sin(ix)$, so identities for $\sin,\cos$
turn into those for $\sinh,\cosh$ by flipping the sign of every product of two
$\sinh$'s (Osborn's rule).

### Derivatives and Integrals

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $\int f(x)\,dx$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\sinh x$ | $\cosh x$ | $\cosh x+C$ |
| $\cosh x$ | $\sinh x$ | $\sinh x+C$ |
| $\tanh x$ | $\operatorname{sech}^2x$ | $\ln\cosh x+C$ |
| $\coth x$ | $-\operatorname{csch}^2x$ | $\ln\lvert\sinh x\rvert+C$ |
| $\operatorname{sech}x$ | $-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x$ | $\arctan(\sinh x)+C$ |
| $\operatorname{csch}x$ | $-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x$ | $\ln\lvert\tanh(x/2)\rvert+C$ |
| $\operatorname{sech}^2x$ | | $\tanh x+C$ |

### Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

| $f(x)$ | Logarithmic form | $f'(x)$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\operatorname{arsinh}x$ | $\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$ | $\dfrac1{\sqrt{x^2+1}}$ |
| $\operatorname{arcosh}x$, $x\ge1$ | $\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)$ | $\dfrac1{\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ |
| $\operatorname{artanh}x$, $\lvert x\rvert<1$ | $\tfrac12\ln\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}$ | $\dfrac1{1-x^2}$ |

with standard integrals ($a>0$)
$$
\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=\operatorname{arsinh}\frac xa+C,\qquad
\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}=\ln\left\lvert x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right\rvert+C,
$$
$$
\int\frac{dx}{a^2-x^2}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left\lvert\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right\rvert+C.
$$

:::{.proof data-title="Derivatives of $\sinh x$ and $\operatorname{arsinh}x$"}

Directly, $(\sinh x)'=\frac{e^x+e^{-x}}{2}=\cosh x$ and likewise
$(\cosh x)'=\sinh x$. For the inverse set $y=\operatorname{arsinh}x$, $x=\sinh y$:
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac1{\cosh y}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+\sinh^2y}}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}},
$$
since $\cosh y>0$.

:::

## Useful Substitutions

Standard integrals involving square roots can be reduced by a
trigonometric or hyperbolic substitution:

| Expression | Substitution | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ | $x=a\sin\theta$ | $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ |
| $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ | $x=a\tan\theta$ or $a\sinh t$ | $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$ |
| $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ | $x=a\sec\theta$ or $a\cosh t$ | $\sec^2\theta-1=\tan^2\theta$ |
| rational in $\sin,\cos$ | $t=\tan(x/2)$ | $\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ |

:::{.example data-title="Area of a Semicircle"}

With $x=a\sin\theta$,
$$
\int_{-a}^a\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}a^2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta
=\frac{a^2}2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(1+\cos2\theta)\,d\theta=\frac{\pi a^2}2.
$$

:::

## Taylor Series

Maclaurin series of the elementary functions ([[taylor-series]]):

| Function | Series | Converges for |
|---|---|---|
| $e^x$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{x^n}{n!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\sin x$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\sinh x$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\cosh x$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$ | all $x$ |
| $\dfrac1{1-x}$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$ ([[geometric-series]]) | $\lvert x\rvert<1$ |
| $\ln(1+x)$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n}$ | $-1<x\le1$ |
| $\arctan x$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{2n+1}$ | $\lvert x\rvert\le1$ |
| $(1+x)^\alpha$ | $\displaystyle\sum_{n\ge0}\binom\alpha nx^n$ | $\lvert x\rvert<1$ |

> *Note:* Comparing the series of $e^x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ term by term
> proves Euler's formula $e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x$. See [[power-series]] and
> [[radius-of-convergence]] for convergence.
